opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and honestly I think a lot of people frame it as an either/or when it's really more of a sequence.

Supervised fine-tuning is the obvious starting point. If you have high-quality demonstrations, a human writing a clean solution to a problem, SFT is very efficient at teaching the model the format, the style, and the basic competence. But the limit becomes clear pretty quickly: with SFT you're bounded by the quality of your annotators. You're asking the model to imitate humans, so at best you get roughly human-level demonstrations, and in practice you get the average of your annotators, including their mistakes.

What surprised me when we started scaling RLHF is that humans are much better at *judging* than at *writing*. I'm not a great poet, but I can tell you which of two poems I prefer. Same with code: it's much cheaper and more reliable for someone to compare two solutions, or to check whether something runs and passes tests, than to write the perfect solution from scratch. And once the model is sometimes producing outputs better than what your annotators would have written, the preference signal lets you push beyond the demonstrations. SFT can't do that.

Code is also a special case because you often have a signal that's even better than human preference: execution. You can run the code, run the unit tests, check whether it compiles, whether it's correct. That's a very clean reward, much harder to hack than a learned reward model, though not impossible, since models will happily overfit to weak tests. So for code, I'd push hard on the RL side, with a mix of execution-based rewards and preference data for the things tests don't capture: readability, sensible structure, good explanations.

So my practical answer: use SFT to bootstrap. Get a decent distribution, the right format, a model that's already sampling reasonable solutions. Then move fairly quickly to RL, because that's where you get the real gains, especially on harder problems where the model has to explore and find solutions nobody demonstrated. A small amount of really high-quality SFT data goes a long way, and beyond that, your annotation budget is usually better spent on comparisons and verifiable feedback than on more demonstrations.

r001.rationale: The response says execution gives code a strong reward signal and recommends RL; it does not explain an intuition that checkable correctness should make SFT preferable.

r002.rationale: It says preference data can capture code qualities that tests miss, including readability and sensible structure.

r003.rationale: It states that RL is where the real gains come after SFT bootstrapping, especially on harder problems.

r004.rationale: The response does not describe a teacher-critic method or human editing of a better bad output into a correct SFT answer.

r005.rationale: The response does not connect human-corrected SFT answers to escaping a local minimum.

fable-5.1.text:
So, the way I think about it — and this really comes from what we learned on Llama 2 and then Llama 3 — is that SFT and RLHF are not really competing, they are answering two different questions.

SFT is about teaching the model the format, the distribution of what a good answer looks like. For code that's actually quite important early on: how do you structure a function, when do you add a comment, how do you respond when the user gives you a vague spec. But SFT has a ceiling, and the ceiling is the quality of your annotators. If I ask a human to write the best possible Python solution, they will write something good, but honestly the model after a few rounds of training is already better than most humans at writing code. So you are distilling something that is below the model's own capability. That was really the surprise for us on Llama 2 — we were spending a lot on SFT data and at some point we realized the model outputs were better than what the humans were writing.

RLHF, or more generally RL with some reward, is the opposite. You don't need the human to produce the answer, you only need them — or a reward model, or a verifier — to recognize which answer is better. And recognizing is much easier than generating. That is the whole trick. For a lot of tasks it's a bit fuzzy, you need preference data, a reward model, and it's noisy. But code is the perfect case, because you have unit tests, you have execution, you have compilers. The reward is almost free and almost perfect. So for code I would push much harder on the RL side than on the SFT side. You generate many samples, you execute them, you keep the ones that pass, and you can either do rejection sampling and fine-tune on them, or go to a proper policy gradient loop. In practice on Llama 3 we did a lot of rejection sampling first because it's simple and stable, and then PPO or DPO on top.

The other thing I would say is: don't underestimate SFT as a bootstrap. If the model never produces a correct sample, your RL signal is zero, you learn nothing. So you need just enough SFT, or enough synthetic data, to get a non-trivial pass rate, and then RL takes over and starts to move the needle. And at that point I would actually generate most of the "SFT" data from the model itself, filtered by execution. Human-written code becomes something you use to teach style and format, not capability.

So if I had to give a rule: SFT to teach the behavior, RL with execution feedback to push the quality, and the moment you have a verifier, trust the verifier more than the annotator.

r001.rationale: The response argues that code’s checkable correctness makes RL with execution feedback preferable; it does not explain an intuition that SFT should be preferable.

r002.rationale: It says some tasks need fuzzy preference data, but does not state that human preferences still arise specifically in code generation despite checkable correctness.

r003.rationale: It says to push much harder on RL than SFT for code and describes execution-based RL as the way to improve quality.

r004.rationale: The response does not describe a teacher-critic method or having a human correct the better of two bad code outputs for SFT.

r005.rationale: The response does not say that human-corrected teacher-critic answers help the model escape a local minimum.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re complementary. With supervised fine-tuning, you show the model a good solution and train it to reproduce that solution. That’s useful for getting started, but in coding there are many valid ways to solve the same problem. Matching one reference answer isn’t necessarily the objective—you want code that works.

Reinforcement learning lets you optimize for that outcome. The model generates code, you execute it, you run tests, and you use the result as feedback. It can discover solutions that weren’t in the demonstrations.

I would distinguish that from RLHF specifically, though. Human feedback can help with things like readability or whether the response follows the user’s intent. But for correctness, coding gives you something very valuable: feedback from execution. So I’d use supervised fine-tuning to establish the behavior, then reinforcement learning where we can reliably measure success. The hard part is making sure the tests actually capture what we want.

r001.rationale: The response says supervised fine-tuning can establish behavior and execution feedback can measure correctness, but does not explain an intuition that checkable code correctness favors supervised fine-tuning over RLHF.

r002.rationale: It says human feedback can help assess readability and whether code follows the user's intent, even though execution can provide correctness feedback.

r003.rationale: It does not claim RLHF generally outperforms supervised fine-tuning; it recommends supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning when success can be measured.

r004.rationale: It does not describe the teacher-critic method or human editing of a better bad output into a correct supervised example.

r005.rationale: It does not discuss human-corrected answers helping the model escape a local minimum.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’re complementary. With supervised fine-tuning, you show the model a solution and ask it to imitate that solution. That’s useful for teaching it how to approach a coding task, but there are many valid ways to write a program. You don’t necessarily want to penalize a correct solution just because it differs from the example.

With reinforcement learning, you can generate a solution, execute it, and reward whether it passes the tests. That gives you a much more direct signal about what you actually care about. And for code, that signal can be easier to verify than asking a human which answer looks better.

So I would usually think of supervised fine-tuning as providing a starting point, and reinforcement learning as improving from there. But I’d distinguish RLHF from reinforcement learning with execution feedback: if you have reliable tests, you don’t need a human preference judgment for every answer. The challenge becomes making sure your tests really capture the task, because the model will optimize whatever you reward.
